clue.text: 'We recognize a— people by the way they sneeze' (Jean Giraudoux)

definitions.text: 'We recognize a— people by the way they sneeze' (Jean Giraudoux)

parts.words: 'We recognize a— people by the way they sneeze' (Jean Giraudoux)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the adjective the French playwright used for a people fated to ruin

explanation.surface: A line from Giraudoux about spotting a nation's fate from its sneezes.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Giraudoux's play about the Trojan War, where the Trojans are a people already fated to fall.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes a people condemned to destruction, the Trojans of the play.

clue.text: Reportedly scarlet woman associated with novelist

explanation.surface: A gossipy remark about a scandalous woman linked to a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scarlet woman' suggests a harlot, but 'reportedly' makes it Scarlett, the heroine of Gone with the Wind, whose surname this is; it is also the surname of the American novelist John O'Hara.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlett of Gone with the Wind bears this surname, as did the American writer John, author of Appointment in Samarra.

clue.text: Invoking the name of Thackeray to settle an argument?

explanation.surface: Someone calls on a Victorian author's name to end a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The novelist's full name was William Makepeace Thackeray.
explanation.definitionFit: Thackeray's middle name; as a phrase it means to end a quarrel and be reconciled.

clue.text: A pastry for Hamlet?

parts.note: the prince Hamlet is from Denmark, so his pastry would be named after his nationality, which is also a sweet breakfast pastry

explanation.surface: Asking what baked treat suits Shakespeare's prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet yeasted breakfast pastry bears the adjective for Denmark, Hamlet's homeland.

clue.text: Cat I provided for Italian poet

parts.note: a leopard is a big cat

explanation.surface: A big cat is given to an Italian poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Giacomo Leopardi was a nineteenth-century Italian lyric poet, author of the Canti.

clue.text: Italian inventor reveals Ovid in a Calderón revision

indicators.note: a revision reworks something into a new form, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
Pedro Calderón de la Barca, the Spanish playwright, taken as written

explanation.surface: A Renaissance genius is uncovered by reworking texts of a Roman poet and a Spanish dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: The page as held drops the final N of Calderón, which the anagram needs: OVID IN A CALDERON has fifteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Renaissance polymath designed flying machines and other devices, so he is famed as an inventor as well as a painter.

clue.text: Macedonian queen seen in London arena on Saturday

parts.note: Olympia is an exhibition and events hall in west London
S is a standard abbreviation for Saturday

explanation.surface: An ancient queen is spotted at a London venue at the weekend.
explanation.walkthrough: OLYMPIA is a large exhibition hall in Kensington, London.
explanation.definitionFit: Olympias was the wife of Philip II of Macedon and mother of Alexander the Great.

clue.text: May be good or bad: Tess's is victim of "his own limitations"

definitions.text: Tess's is victim of "his own limitations"

explanation.surface: A note on a character in Hardy's novel undone by his own failings.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles her husband is Angel Clare, whom Hardy calls the victim of his own limitations when he rejects her.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirits of heaven or hell can be good or fallen; Tess's husband in Hardy's novel bears this first name.

clue.text: A rude Muir reinvented as novelist

indicators.note: reinventing something reshapes it entirely, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An impolite Scottish writer is reborn as a different author.
explanation.definitionFit: Daphne du Maurier wrote Rebecca and other popular novels.

clue.text: One of 14 who might spoil a philosopher, only lacking a pupil

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
Immanuel Kant, the German philosopher

indicators.note: lacking means going without, so the pupil is dropped from the word beside it

parts.note: L, the learner plate, stands for a pupil driver

explanation.surface: Someone among a group could ruin a thinker, though just short of a student.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 is the answer at 14-down, TRIUMVIRI; Mark Antony was one of the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus. ONLY loses its L to give ONY.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Antony shared power in Rome's Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus, making him one of its three rulers.

clue.text: A pastime of A. S. Byatt

explanation.surface: A hobby belonging to a British novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: The Game is A. S. Byatt's 1967 novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A sport or amusement is a pastime; The Game is the title of Byatt's second novel.

clue.text: Mass rape disaster for daughter of river-god and mother of Cleopatra

definitions.text: daughter of river-god and mother of Cleopatra

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things in ruins and disorder, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A violent catastrophe befalls a figure of Greek myth.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth she was the daughter of the river-god Evenus and mother of Cleopatra, the wife of Meleager, not the Egyptian queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Marpessa, daughter of Evenus, married Idas and bore Cleopatra, later wife of Meleager.

clue.text: Twin, and star in his own right

explanation.surface: A twin who shines on his own merit.
explanation.walkthrough: Pollux is one of the twins Castor and Pollux, and also the brightest star in Gemini.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the immortal Dioscuri twin of Castor, and a bright star in the constellation Gemini carries his name.

clue.text: Oast rebuilt in Greek portico

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the parts together again in a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hop kiln is reconstructed inside a Greek colonnade.
explanation.walkthrough: An OAST is a kiln for drying hops, familiar in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered colonnade in ancient Greece where people met and walked, as the Stoics did.

clue.text: Seen in the atrium, virile leaders of men

indicators.note: seen in means the letters can be spotted inside the clue words that follow

explanation.surface: Manly chiefs are spotted in a Roman hall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin plural for members of a ruling board of three, who led Rome in the late Republic.

clue.text: Scandinavian magic circle

parts.note: reads like a club of Nordic conjurers, but describes an enchanted ring of Norse myth

explanation.surface: A Nordic society of stage magicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The Magic Circle is a British society of conjurers; here a circle is a ring, Odin's gold ring that drips eight more every ninth night.
explanation.definitionFit: In Norse myth Odin's self-multiplying gold arm-ring bears this name, an enchanted band from the North.

clue.text: Patrick O'Neill's Letter of Marque legalized one

definitions.text: Patrick O'Neill's Letter of Marque legalized one

parts.words: Patrick O'Neill's Letter of Marque legalized one
parts.note: a letter of marque was a licence letting a private ship's captain attack enemy shipping, the subject of the naval novel named

explanation.surface: A novel's title document made a seafarer lawful.
explanation.walkthrough: The novel is The Letter of Marque, by Patrick O'Brian, as the clue prints the author's name; in it Jack Aubrey sails under such a licence.
explanation.definitionFit: An armed private ship or its captain licensed by government to capture enemy vessels, rather than a pirate.

clue.text: The only decent one is a deaf Trappist, thought John Le Carré

definitions.text: The only decent one is a deaf Trappist, thought John Le Carré

parts.words: The only decent one is a deaf Trappist, thought John Le Carré
parts.note: the spy novelist's quip about envoys: the only good one says nothing and hears nothing, like a silent monk

explanation.surface: A spy novelist's cynical remark about a profession.
explanation.walkthrough: Trappist monks keep a vow of silence; Le Carré, a former Foreign Office man, said the only decent member of the profession is a deaf Trappist.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy representing a state abroad, the profession Le Carré mocked.

clue.text: Baltimore oriole identified by Stravinsky

explanation.surface: A songbird is named by a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: The Baltimore oriole is a bright orange North American bird; Stravinsky's ballet of 1910 shares the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The orange-and-black songbird has this folk name, and Stravinsky's 1910 ballet is called this.

clue.text: Pill-box in main road

indicators.note: in means the letters are found inside the clue words that follow

explanation.surface: A concrete pillbox stands on a highway.
explanation.walkthrough: A pillbox suggests a gun emplacement; here it is a small box for pills.
explanation.definitionFit: A small Japanese lacquered case of compartments, hung from the sash, for carrying medicines.

clue.text: It's common in a book

parts.note: points to the Anglican service book titled the Book of Common something, the word after common

explanation.surface: Something ordinary found in literature.
explanation.walkthrough: The Book of Common Prayer is the Church of England's service book.
explanation.definitionFit: A petition to God, the word following common in the Anglican service book's title.

clue.text: Fairy story will contain it, but not be it

definitions.text: Fairy story will contain it, but not be it

parts.words: Fairy story will contain it, but not be it
parts.note: a fable holds a lesson about right conduct, yet the tale itself never lacks ethics

explanation.surface: A riddle about what a fairy tale holds but cannot itself be.
explanation.walkthrough: Split after its first letter, the word is the lesson a fairy story contains; read whole, meaning without ethics, it is what such a story is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking any sense of right and wrong, the opposite of the lesson a fable teaches.

clue.text: Historian and inseparable companion of Trevor ()

explanation.surface: A scholar who always goes about with his friend.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Trevor-Roper was a British historian, so the surname is joined by hyphen to Trevor.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Trevor-Roper, the Oxford historian, had this as the second half of his surname, always hyphened to Trevor.

clue.text: The French I discovered in sci-fi writer recalls Parnassian poet

indicators.note: something discovered in a place is found inside it, so the French article and I go inside the writer

parts.note: Jules Verne, the French pioneer of science fiction
la is the French feminine for the

explanation.surface: A French phrase found in Jules Verne recalls a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Parnassians were a group of nineteenth-century French poets with whom Verlaine was first associated.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Verlaine began among the Parnassian group of French poets before turning Symbolist.

clue.text: Roman date is not any Sunday

parts.note: none means not any

explanation.surface: A claim that a Roman calendar day never falls on a Sunday.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the seventh day of March, May, July and October, the fifth of other months.

clue.text: Silver identifying mark

parts.note: reads like a hallmark on silverware, but means the telltale gait of the one-legged pirate Long John Silver

explanation.surface: A hallmark stamped on silver plate.
explanation.walkthrough: Long John Silver, the one-legged pirate of Treasure Island, is known by his halting walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A halting, uneven gait such as a one-legged pirate on a crutch would have.

clue.text: Cash (not a lot) for Fleming secretary

parts.note: money is cash
a penny is a very small sum

explanation.surface: A modest sum handed to a novelist's assistant.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss Moneypenny is M's secretary in Ian Fleming's James Bond novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Miss Moneypenny works for M in Ian Fleming's Bond books, a personal assistant at MI6.

clue.text: Sung words bring it back to free French model

parts.note: libre is the French for free
T as in the Model T Ford

indicators.note: back means the word it is read backwards

explanation.surface: Songs bring a liberated French fashion model home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free French' looks like de Gaulle's wartime movement but is the French word for free; 'back' turns the word it, and 'bring it ... to' sets that after the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The texts of operas, the words set to music and sung, in the Italian plural.

clue.text: "My train are men of choice and — parts" (King Lear)

definitions.text: "My train are men of choice and — parts" (King Lear)

parts.words: "My train are men of choice and — parts" (King Lear)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank line from Lear's defence of his knights: the missing word is the superlative of uncommon

explanation.surface: Lear boasts of the quality of his retinue.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear says his knights are men of choice and the most exceptional parts, that is, qualities.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative meaning most uncommon or finest, describing the knights' qualities.
